text: This is the Continuous Compliance Framework, running a demo for a fictional bank, Meridian Financial Group. It tracks ten systems, with live evidence from GitHub and Kubernetes.
You can sign in with a local account, or with single sign-on through Google, LDAP or GitHub.
Everything starts with evidence. Agents and plugins check your systems continuously, and send in the results.
Each check is stored as evidence, with a pass or fail status, labels that say where it came from, and when it was last seen.
Let's open a failing check: the default repository permission for the GitHub organisation.
The evidence says what it tests, and why it failed. It's signed, so it can't be quietly altered, and its history shows how the result has changed over time.
Each of Meridian's systems has its own System Security Plan.
We'll pick the Customer Portal to work in.
The compliance page shows how the Customer Portal measures up against each of its control profiles: which controls are satisfied, which aren't, and how many are implemented.
Implementation records how each of those controls is met for this system.
The compliance map ties it all together: from the corporate standard, through policies, down to the controls and the evidence behind them.
Every node rolls up compliance and open risk from the nodes below it.
Let's drill down through the resilience policy, to one control: production workloads must span multiple availability zones.
This control is seventy-one percent met. The failures are linked to risks, such as a legacy batch job that runs in a single availability zone.
Opening the control shows it across all ten systems: which pass, which fail, and which are out of scope.
The graph view shows the same map, ordered by open risk, worst first.
Failing evidence feeds a risk register for each system.
The dashboard shows the Customer Portal's risks by status, and a heatmap of likelihood against impact.
In the register, risks can be filtered and reviewed, accepted with a justification, or promoted to a plan of action and milestones.
Not all evidence comes from machines. Workflows record recurring human processes, such as access reviews and disaster recovery exercises.
Each system has its own scheduled workflows, each with a cadence and owners.
This is the quarterly access review for the workforce identity provider. Each step is assigned to a role, and completing it produces evidence.
That's the Continuous Compliance Framework: evidence collected continuously, and mapped from controls, to policies, to standards.
